Gastrointestinal Involvement in Neurologic 
Disorders: Stiff-Man and Charcot-Marie-Tooth 
Syndromes 
IRFAN SOYKAN, MD, RICHARD W. McCALLUM, MD, FACP, FACG 
ABSTRACT: Many neurologic conditions can 
affect the striated muscle of the gastrointesti­
nal tract, resulting in dysphagia. In this arti­
cle, two patients with rare neurologic disor­
ders are reported (Stiff-man syndrome and 
Charcot-Marie-Tooth syndrome). Both pa­
tients had pharyngeal dysphagia. In addition, 
there was evidence of smooth muscle involve­
ment in other areas of the gastrointestinal 
tract, specifically abnormal esophageal motil­
ity and delayed gastric emptying. In the En­
glish literature, there are only two reports of 
Stiff-man syndrome and dysphagia, and there 
are no reports of Charcot-Marie-Tooth syn­
drome. These represent the first accounts of 
smooth muscle dysfunction in those uncom­
mon neurologic disorders. KEY INDEXING 
TERMS: Stiff-man syndrome; Charcot-Marie­
Tooth syndrome; Gastric emptying; Esopha­
geal motility; Cisapride. [Am J Med Sci 
1997;313(1):70-73.] 
Neuromuscular disorders ofthe gastrointestinal 
(GI) tract are poorly recognized; thus, diagno­
sis and treatment are often delayed and costly.1 
Many neurologic conditions that are thought primar­
ily to involve striated muscle also can display vari­
ous gastrointestinal manifestations. Stiff-man syn­
drome (SMS), a rare cause of oropharyngeal dyspha­
gia, is a dramatic central nervous system disease 
characterized by continuous muscle rigidity and 
painful spasms that resembles a long-term form of

tetanus. 2•3 Another disease, Charcot-Marie-Tooth 
(CMT) syndrome, is one of the most frequently inher­
ited causes of neurologic disability. The most promi­
nent features of CMT are gradually progressive dis­
tal muscle weakness and atrophy.4 Gastrointestinal 
system involvement with both diseases is rare. Only 
two cases ofGI involvement have been reported that 
were related to SMS and dysphagia, but no cases of 
CMT syndrome were reported with GI involve­
ment. 5•6 We recently evaluated two adult patients; 
one had SMS and the other had CMT syndrome. We 
report our observations of the concomitant abnor­
malities of striated and smooth muscle in these rare 
entities. 
Case Reports 
Case 1. The patient is a 34-year-old woman who has had symp­
toms consistent with SMS for more than 12 years but was diag­
nosed only recently (approximately 1 year ago) with it. The pa­
tient was treated with plasmapheresis and cyclophosphamide. 
She had two courses of plasmapheresis with symptomatic relief 
of her muscle spasms for approximately 2 months. Each course 
consisted of approximately six exchanges. The patient was re­
ferred from the neurology outpatient unit because of her GI com­
plaints. Her main complaint was constipation. She had some up­
per GI symptoms that included nausea, early satiety, and mild 
reflux symptoms. In addition, she had pharyngeal dysphagia, an 
intermittent hold-up of food in the pharynx. Abdominal films

showed no evidence of bowel dilation. The results of an anorectal 
motility study were normal-negative for sphincteric function. A 
gastric-emptying study using an isotope-labeled solid meal 
(chicken liver and beef stew) showed delayed gastric emptying. 
The time it took to empty 50% of the meal (T%) was 221 minutes. 
The percentage of solids retained at 120 minutes was 76% (normal 
values for T % and percent of retention at 2 hours are respectively, 
<150 minutes and <70%). An upper GI endoscopy and esopha­
geal motility study were not performed because of her painful 
muscle spasms secondary to SMS. Organic lesions, which can 
cause delayed gastric emptying, were excluded by barium studies. 
She had hypothyroidism that was controlled with hormone re­
placement. 
The patient began therapy with a prokinetic agent (10 mg cisa­
pride four times a day). In addition, 1 oz magnesium citrate daily 
was given to ease constipation. The patient was followed up for 
approximately 1 year. During the follow-up period, she continued 
to take cisapride 10 mg four times a day to increase motility 
throughout the gut and metoclopramide for nausea. The patient 
continued to have some degree of breakthrough nausea and vom­
iting approximately once or twice a week. Overall her weight was 
stable.

Figure 1. Esophageal motility tracing with the top four leads 
spaced 5 cm apart in the body of the esophagus, one lead in the 
lower esophageal sphincter and the lowest lead is in the stomach. 
All are constantly perfused by a pneumohydraulic system. Three 
wet swallows are represented and indicate both peristaltic and 
nonperistaltic contractions are occurring. The amplitude of the 
contractions is lower in the proximal two leads. The pressure 
in the lower esophageal sphincter was <10 mm Hg and hence 
decreased with normal swallow-induced relaxations. 
Case 2. A 28-year-old man with a 3-year history of CMT syn­
drome was evaluated for symptoms consistent with GI motility 
disorder. His uncle and a brother had CMT, and there was con­
cern about the brother's son having CMT. The patient complained 
of abdominal and chest pain, which he explained as a tight feeling 
across his abdomen and his chest. He had intermittent pharyn­
geal dysphagia. Although he had no specific gastroesophageal 
reflux or heartburn symptoms, he experienced some nocturnal 
wheezing, occasional morning hoarseness, and increased dental 
caries. He also complained of degrees of nausea and feelings of 
"a rumbling GI tract," suggestive of borborygmus. In the past, he 
was treated with various acid-blocking agents and the motility 
agents, cisapride and metoclopramide, with no changes in his 
condition. An upper endoscopy demonstrated mild distal esopha­
gitis. The results of an upper GI barium swallow showed no abnor­
mality. A gastric-emptying study using an isotope-labeled solid 
meal (egg) showed delayed gastric emptying with a T% of 153 
minutes. The upper limit of normal for an egg meal is 150 min­
utes. An esophageal motility study showed a decrease in peristal­
sis to 50% in the smooth muscle portion of the esophagus. Peri­
stalsis normally should be greater than 70%. There was also a 
decrease in the contraction amplitude of the esophagus, and the 
lower esophageal sphincter pressure was 5 mm Hg (normally it 
is 15 mm Hg to 40 mm Hg). Esophageal contraction amplitudes 
that were 2 cm, 7 cm, and 12 cm above the lower esophageal 
sphincter site were 46.6 mm Hg (range, 0 to 80 mm Hg, normal, 
50 to 180 mm Hg), 25.2 mm Hg (range, 0 to 44 mm Hg, normal, 
50 to 150 mm Hg), and 9.6 mm Hg (range, 0 to 16 mm Hg, normal, 
50 to 150 mm Hg) respectively (Figure 1). During the Bernstein 
test and the injection of edrophonium chloride (Tensilon, ICN 
Pharmaceuticals, Costa Mesa, CA), the patient had pain indica­
tive of a very sensitive esophagus. 
The patient was administered promethazine and ondansetron 
for nausea. This produced a resolution of the nausea, and we 
decided to administer 100 mg amitriptyline at night to address 
the visceral afferent sensitivity. During his last visit, it was de­
cided that the amitriptyline had not worked. His weight was sta­
ble, and although he had some dysphagia, food and nutrition did 
not seem to cause a problem. He had occasional nocturnal 
coughing and gastroesophageal reflux. This was not surprising 
given the motility result described. Because of this abnormal mo-

tility the patient was administered 10 mg metoclopramide four 
times a day to be taken orally as tolerated to address abnormal 
upper GI motility. This approach reduced his gastroesophageal 
reflux symptoms and further reduced the nausea. 
Discussion 
In 1956, Moersch and Woltman 7 reported their

findings of a 32-year study of 14 patients with invol­
untary muscle stiffness of axial musculature and su­
perimposed spasms. The term SMS originally was 
coined by Moersch and Woltman because 83% of the 
patients in the study were men; however, SMS can 
affect both sexes and may be more appropriately 
called stiff-person syndrome. 8 The cause of SMS is 
unclear, but the pathologic site probably is located 
in the brain stem and the spinal cord anterior horn 
cells. Two neurotransmitters responsible for control­
ling impulse activity to the skeleton are norepineph­
rine and gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA). The 
balance between norepinephrine and GABA is im­
paired because an immunoglobulin G class autoanti­
body is directed against glutamic acid decarboxylase, 
an enzyme needed for the synthesis of GABA. Too 
much norepinephrine at anterior hom cell synaptic 
junctions causes axial and limb muscles to contract 
continuously and fuse into a singular sustained con­
traction. 9 Many researchers have reported an associ­
ation among SMS, epilepsy, endocrine diseases such 
as insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus, and various 
organ specific autoimmune disorders that include 
Graves' diseases, pernicious anemia, and vitiligo. 
Autoantibodies in serum and cerebrospinal fluid 
acted against glutamic acid decarboxylase, and pan­
creatic islet cells have been detected in some pa­
tients with SMS.10 - 13 Our patient had hypothyroid­
ism, which was controlled. Credible evidence of GI 
dysmotility was found in the esophagus, the stom­
ach, and the large intestine. In 1970, Sulway et al5 
reported a patient with SMS and complete esopha­
geal obstruction. No disease was found after an en­
doscopy. The patient responded dramatically to diaz­
epam, and had complete relief of the obstruction. 
Bhutani 6 studied a second patient with dysphagia. 
After the patient was diagnosed with SMS and ther­
apy with high doses of oral diazepam was instituted, 
the dysphagia was cured and has never recurred. 
Both patients experienced pharyngeal dysphagia 
and intermittent hold-up offood in the pharynx and 
the upper esophagus consistent with the potential 
involvement of striated muscle in the swallowing 
process. Oropharyngeal dysphagia is characterized 
by the impaired ability to transfer food from the 
mouth to the upper esophagus and is suggested by 
symptoms such as coughing or choking while eating, 
difficulty in swallowing, and nasal regurgitation of 
liquids. The sensation of dysphagia commonly occurs 
as a manifestation of a neuromuscular disorder; the 
underlying course often is suggested by a careful 
history and physical examination. 14

Gastrointestinal Tractus in Neurologic Disorders 
Many neurologic conditions may affect the smooth 
muscle of the alimentary tract. Multiple sclerosis 
is a focal demyelinating neurologic disorder of the 
central nervous system. It is associated with gastric 
retention and colonic dysmotility.15 Muscular dystro­
phies are inherited myopathies that feature progres­
sive weakness and muscle wasting. They have been 
subclassified into a number of syndromes based on 
clinical and genetic evidence. In myotonic muscular 
dystrophy, GI symptoms are prominent. Decreased 
peristalsis throughout the body and the antrum of 
the stomach was observed. It was postulated that 
abnormal gastric motility was a predisposition to the 
formation of food concretions. 16 Duchenne's muscu­
lar dystrophy, in which functional impairment of 
smooth muscle in the GI tract can cause acute gas­
tric dilatation and intestinal pseudo-obstruction, 
may be fatal. 17 Oculopharyngeal muscular dystro­
phy predominantly affects the striated muscle of the 
GI tract and is characterized by ptosis and dyspha­
gia. 1S Polymyositis and dermatomyositis may be as­
sociated with the motor dysfunction of the entire GI 
tract. Delayed gastric and esophageal emptying are 
common in polymyositis and dermatomyositis and 
imply frequent malfunction of the smooth muscle 
of the upper GI tract. 19 Patients with Parkinson's 
disease often have GI symptoms caused by either 
motor abnormalities of the GI tract related to Par­
kinson's disease or the side effects of therapy with 
dopamine agonists. Gastric emptying time also is 
delayed in Parkinson's disease. 2o Our patients with 
SMS and CMT syndrome experienced upper GI 
symptoms such as nausea and early satiety. When 
an isotope-labeled solid meal was used, both patients 
showed delayed gastric emptying implying smooth 
muscle involvement of the GI tract. 
Little information about the pathologic basis of 
GI involvement in neurologic diseases is available. 
Examination of the myenteric plexus in the colon 
and the megacolon of a patient with myotonic dystro­
phy revealed degeneration and decreased numbers 
of argyrophilic neurons and axons. 21 Autopsy studies 
in a small number of patients with myotonic dystro­
phy have shown changes such as swelling, destruc­
tion, and fatty infiltration in the smooth muscle cells 
of the GI tract. 22 It is thought that smooth muscle 
dysfunction is a predominant cause of GI dysmotility 
in most patients with muscular dystrophies. 23 The 
finding of Lewy bodies in the esophageal myenteric 
plexus of patients with Parkinson's disease and dys­
phagia and in patients with achalasia suggests that 
neuronal degeneration may be responsible for esoph­
ageal dysfunction. 24 In the patient with CMT syn­
drome, impaired peristalsis of the esophagus was 
consistent with myenteric plexus involvement. Re­
view of the literature revealed no data regarding GI 
involvement in CMT syndrome. Our report of esoph­
ageal and gastric smooth muscle impairments repre-

sents the first observation. Theoretically, this dis­
ease is dominated by striated muscle dysfunction, 
but it has been seen in a number of neurologic disor­
ders that there can be degrees of smooth muscle 
involvement. 4 The patient with SMS was treated 
with the prokinetic agent cisapride to help motility 
from the esophagus to the colon and with magne­
sium citrate for constipation. After treatment, the 
patient's weight was stable, and dysphagia, early

satiety, nausea and constipation were under control. 
The patient with CMT syndrome was treated with 
promethazine and ondansetron (centrally acting an­
tiemetics) that helped partially. Metoclopramide 
was added to this therapy to treat his abnormal up­
per GI motility. These patients would be good candi­
dates for treatment with domperidone, a dopamine 
antagonist that has no central nervous system ef­
fects related to the dopamine receptor blockade, al­
though it is a potent antiemetic at the chemoreceptor 
trigger zone and is a prokinetic for the esophagus, 
the stomach, and the small bowel. 21,25 
In summary, we presented two unusual neurologic 
disorders with GI involvement. Many neurologic dis­
turbances can affect the striated and the smooth 
muscle of the GI tract resulting in GI dysmotility. 
Gastroenterologists and neurologists should be 
aware that GI dysfunction may occur in patients 
with neurologic disorders.
